lines.text: Why does almost every country on Earth use red, yellow, and green for traffic signals?
The system dates back to nineteenth-century British railway signals.
Red has the longest wavelength of any visible light spectrum.
This means red scatters the least in rain and dense fog, allowing drivers to spot danger from the farthest distance.
Railroads originally used clear white light for 'go', but drivers mistook stars or streetlamps for signals.
So engineers adopted green for safety, and later added bright yellow as a transition warning.
That nineteenth-century railroad color code keeps hundreds of millions of drivers safe today.
